abstract: Coded in Julia using ModelingToolkit, we developed a new computational model (TeMP) that calculates the emergent physiological responses to heat with and without physical activity (PA). Rooted in established physical and physiological principles, we detail the model framework, major novelties, and sources of individual variation. TeMP uses physical heat-transfer and heat-balance concepts to determine the rate of whole-body heat storage (S) over a given exposure period, based on the dynamic relationship between S, tissue temperature, and thermoeffector function. Each thermoeffector (skin blood flow, sweating, and ventilation) operates on independent feedback loops and is modelled based on afferent inputs from central and peripheral/skin tissue temperatures. All thermoeffectors use simple piecewise equations to determine the onset threshold, slope, and maximum functions, removing the need for a central error signal pervasive in alternative models. Skin blood flow is bounded by individual fitness level and is attenuated by PA, whereas sweating is more sensitive during PA due to heightened sympathetic activity. Minute ventilation is also bounded by individual fitness and is sensitive to body temperature and PA intensity, capturing the disproportionate increase in breathing rate at the ventilatory threshold. Thermoeffector functions are individualised for intrinsic characteristics, including heat acclimatisation, age, menstrual cycle phase, skin grafting, sympathetic blockade (i.e., spinal cord lesion), and severe energy restriction (i.e., anorexia nervosa). Finally, heart and rectal temperature are modelled independently and follow similar divergent patterns shown in empirical studies at rest and during PA.
